title: Roland Holden and his Doll Dance routine
summary: Green recalls Bradley student Roland Holden, who built a lovely routine on one step to Doll Dance in spats and high hat.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Who else would you say you were great friends with, like at the time of the Hoofers Club, or -- was anybody else inspiring you other than John Bubbles?

Yes, there was Roland Holden. He used to -- that was one of Buddy Bradley's students. And I tell you, I think Mr. Bradley called him 'hookey player', see, because he was a cute little man, and he was a great friend, you know. We were good buddies, you see.
How did he inspire you, Roland Holden?

Well, he used to dance to this famous melody. All the pianists used to like to play this. They called it "Nola", or, "Doll Dance" (singing), or "Kitten on the Keys". It's like a doll dancing, you see. And he had a way of -- he wore these spats and patent leather shoes, you know, and he was in the high hat and tails, you see. Or either he'd talk, you know. But his tap dancing, I thought, I thought it was splendid to watch and listen to, and I liked it.
What was it that really took your eye and your ear?

It was one of the steps that he got from his class, from his dancing class, you see, with the Buddy Bradley, you know, lessons. And when he just got that one step, you know, and he built a tap routine around it and chose this piece, the "Doll Dance".
What do you think the difference was with that step? Was it the way it was paced or the style of it?
Yes. It was very loving, you see. It was just like being caressed by a soft breeze, you know. Of course you would like to see it, you would like to hear it over and over again, you see.
